t: 井の中の蛙大海を知らず
r: いのなかのかわずたいかいをしらず
mean: someone in a small world who thinks it is the whole world
lit: the frog in the well does not know the great sea

story.text: In the 'Autumn Floods' chapter of the Zhuangzi, the god of the Yellow River is proud of his swollen river until he reaches the sea and sees no end to it. The spirit of the North Sea tells him that you cannot talk about the sea to a frog in a well, because it is confined to its little space. The Japanese saying comes from this image.

use.how: Said of someone whose small surroundings made them overconfident, often of oneself in hindsight; often shortened: 私は井の中の蛙だった。

cue: A boy who was the best player in his small town joins a national academy and finds dozens of players far better than him.

t: 三人寄れば文殊の知恵

bad.s: 被害[ひがい]が大[おお]きすぎて、少[すこ]しの寄付[きふ]では{寝耳[ねみみ]に水[みず]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: the damage is so great that a small donation won't help)

r: りょうやくはくちににがし
mean: good advice, like good medicine, is unpleasant to take
lit: good medicine tastes bitter in the mouth

story.text: In the Kongzi Jiayu (The School Sayings of Confucius), Confucius says that good medicine is bitter in the mouth but benefits the illness, and that loyal advice grates on the ear but benefits one's conduct. The Japanese proverb keeps the first half; the advice it stands for is the second.

use.how: Quoted to accept or justify harsh but useful criticism: 良薬は口に苦しと言うから、彼の意見を聞こう。 Said by the one receiving it, or to soften one's own criticism.

cue: Your editor tears your first chapter apart. It stings, but you realise every point would make the book better.

ctx.s: 先輩[せんぱい]の注意[ちゅうい]は厳[きび]しいけど、{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}だと思[おも]って聞[き]いている。
ctx.en: My senior's criticism is harsh, but I listen, telling myself that what's good for you is hard to swallow.

ctx.s: 「部長[ぶちょう]にかなり厳[きび]しく言[い]われたよ。」「{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}って言[い]うじゃない。」
ctx.en: "The boss gave me a real dressing-down." "Well, good advice is bitter medicine, as they say."

ctx.s: コーチの言葉[ことば]は痛[いた]かったが、{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}で、おかげで試合[しあい]に勝[か]てた。
ctx.en: The coach's words hurt, but they were the bitter medicine I needed, and thanks to them we won the match.

ctx.s: 友人[ゆうじん]は「{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}だから、はっきり言[い]うね」と言[い]って、私[わたし]の欠点[けってん]を挙[あ]げた。
ctx.en: Saying "The truth hurts, but it's good for you, so I'll be blunt," my friend listed my faults.

ctx.en: It's the opinions that are hard to hear that we should value most. Isn't good medicine always bitter?

ctx.s: お客様[きゃくさま]からの厳[きび]しい評価[ひょうか]も、{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}と受[う]け止[と]め、改善[かいぜん]に生[い]かしてまいります。
ctx.en: We take even our customers' harsh reviews as bitter but useful medicine and will put them to use in improving.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は口[くち]が悪[わる]くて、いつも人[ひと]の悪口[わるくち]ばかり言[い]う。{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}だ。
bad.en: (meant: he has a nasty tongue and is always bad-mouthing people)
bad.why: It is about criticism that is hard to hear but does you good; plain spite and gossip are not good medicine.

bad.s: 上司[じょうし]に褒[ほ]められて、{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}でとても嬉[うれ]しかった。
bad.en: (meant: I was really happy to be praised by my boss)
bad.why: It is only about bitter, unwelcome words that help you; praise is the opposite.

r: みつごのたましいひゃくまで
mean: the character formed in early childhood lasts a lifetime
lit: the soul of a three-year-old lasts until a hundred (mitsugo here is a three-year-old, not triplets)

use.how: A comment on a trait or habit someone has had since early childhood and still shows: 三つ子の魂百までで、今も負けず嫌いだ。 Also used to stress early upbringing.

near.diff: 蛙の子は蛙 says a child is like its parents; 三つ子の魂百まで says a person's own early character does not change.

cue: As a toddler you lined up your toys by colour, and at thirty you still sort your bookshelf exactly the same way.

ctx.en: My little brother has loved sweet things ever since he was tiny. What you are as a toddler you stay for life.

ctx.en: Dad has hated losing since he was a child, and he still gets cross when he loses a game. The child is father of the man.
